extracted.intended_audience: state regulators, public water system operators, stakeholders (industry, public health, environmental groups), and public commenters on the proposed perchlorate NPDWR
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble and guidance for the EPA's proposed National Primary Drinking Water Regulation (NPDWR) for perchlorate, including standards for evidence review, derivation of toxicity values (RfD, POD, BMR), MCLG/MCL development, monitoring, analytical methods, compliance, and public reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject to Unbiased Peer Review
rubrics_metrics.description: During the EPA's systematic review process, studies are identified from peer-reviewed literature databases agnostic of results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process must be transparently documented (literature identification and screening). Foundational science and modeling approaches should be based on peer-reviewed literature and undergo multiple independent external peer review processes (e.g., SAB and independent peer review panels). See literature identification in section 3.4.1.1 and literature screening in 3.4.1.2 (USEPA, 2025b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepting of Negative Results as Positive Outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA's systematic review method for identifying literature is agnostic to results; studies reporting null findings or significant findings are considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative results must be included during study evaluation, evidence determination and integration, and uncertainty characterization. Evidence integration should consider negative or inconsistent results and apply appropriate evidence determinations (e.g., evidence inadequate). Example: two of three health outcomes were determined to have inadequate evidence (cardiovascular and neurological) after considering negative/inconsistent results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Without Conflicts of Interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps must be taken throughout the structured systematic review process to ensure the development of the health assessment is without conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific steps include using peer-reviewed literature databases, transparent documentation of the systematic review process and results, using studies agnostic of results, and evaluating studies for potential bias. Peer-reviewed journals' COI statements help minimize COI; in unusual circumstances EPA may require additional independent peer review to meet Information Quality guideline COI requirements (see Final Information Quality Bulletin for Peer Review) (OMB, 2005).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct fit-for-purpose Systematic Reviews per EPA Methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic reviews must be performed according to the Agency's peer-reviewed systematic review methods to identify the best available science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design reviews to identify human epidemiological and animal toxicological data relevant to specified health outcome categories (endocrine, neurological, cardiovascular, cancer) or focused relationships (e.g., maternal T4 and neurodevelopment). Document methods and results in the draft health effects TSD; select critical studies that remain best available to inform modeling approaches (example: Korevaar et al., 2016 selected as critical study).

rubrics_metrics.name: Select Benchmark Response (BMR) Consistent with Guidance and Data
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a BMR based on biological significance, observable range of health effects data, and statistical power of the critical study, consistent with EPA Benchmark Dose Technical Guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider multiple candidate BMRs (e.g., 1%, 2%, 3% decreases in mean IQ); use a 1% BMR for epidemiology data when supported (EPA guidance: 'a BMR of 1% has typically been used for quantal human data from epidemiology studies'). Do not perform BMD modeling below 1% when guidance offers no recommendations and data resolution (e.g., IQ reported as integers) places BMR below observable range. See section 5.2.4 of the draft TSD.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive POD and Apply Appropriate Uncertainty Factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive a point of departure (POD) using the chosen BMR and dose-response modeling (e.g., BBDR model), then apply a total uncertainty factor (UF) to account for population variability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: POD of 3.1 μg/kg/day from 2-step BBDR model and 1% BMR; apply total UF of 3 to produce human-equivalent POD to derive draft RfD. Use Agency peer-reviewed human health risk assessment methods for selecting UFs (USEPA, 2002a). Round toxicity values to one significant figure per Agency best practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round Toxicity Values and MCLGs to One Significant Figure
rubrics_metrics.description: Round RfD and MCLG values to one significant figure according to Agency best practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow cited best practice (APHA, 1992; Brinker and Wolf, 1984; USEPA, 2000a). Example: draft RfD rounded to 1 μg/kg/day and proposed MCLG rounded to 0.02 mg/L (20 μg/L).

rubrics_metrics.name: Define MCLG Using Most Sensitive Populations and Specific Inputs
rubrics_metrics.description: The MCLG is the level at which no known or anticipated adverse effects occur and which allows an adequate margin of safety; in deriving it, EPA considers effects on the general and sensitive populations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the most sensitive life stage/population (example: offspring of hypothyroxinemic pregnant women in first trimester). Inputs for noncancer MCLG include oral noncancer toxicity value (RfD), body weight-adjusted drinking water intake (DWI-BW), and relative source contribution (RSC). Example values: DWI-BW for females 13 to <50 years = 0.0354 L/kg/day; RSC calculated as 80% based on draft RfD.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Best Available Peer-Reviewed Science and Account for Uncertainty in Benefit-Cost Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: In implementing SDWA section 1412, EPA must use the best available, peer-reviewed science and consider data quality and uncertainties in benefit-cost analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document the science, studies relied upon, and how uncertainty affects analysis in the preamble and associated TSDs; consider changes in science between determinations and proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate Feasibility of MCLs via Analytical Methods and Treatment Technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: When setting the MCL as close to the MCLG as feasible, evaluate the feasibility of chemical analysis at drinking water laboratories and available treatment technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider method minimum reporting levels (MRLs), method performance under lab conditions, likelihood of utilization among certified labs, analytical costs, and field performance and cost-affordability of treatment technologies (examples: ion exchange, biological treatment, reverse osmosis demonstrated to achieve high removal efficiency). Use these evaluations to determine feasible MCL alternatives (e.g., 20, 40, 80 µg/L).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish HRRCA and Analyze Alternative MCLs
rubrics_metrics.description: When proposing an MCL, EPA must publish and seek comment on the Health Risk Reduction and Cost Analysis (HRRCA) for the proposed MCL and each alternative considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HRRCA must include quantifiable and nonquantifiable health risk reduction benefits of MCL compliance, benefits of reduced exposure to co-occurring contaminants, quantifiable and nonquantifiable costs, incremental costs and benefits of alternatives, effects on general and sensitive populations, and other factors such as data quality and uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occurrence Assessment Using Statistical Models Incorporating Detects and Non-Detects
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate contaminant occurrence by combining datasets (e.g., UCMR and State compliance data) into a model that uses all suitable observed data, including non-detects, to produce probabilistic exposure estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example approach: Bayesian hierarchical model used to estimate number of systems and populations exposed above proposed MCLs; approach consistent with prior rulemakings (PFAS, arsenic, Cryptosporidium). Refer to Perchlorate Occurrence and Monitoring Report for full analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop and Approve Analytical Methods Meeting Performance and Utilization Criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose analytical methods for identification and quantification of the contaminant that meet method performance under relevant lab conditions and are likely to be used by certified drinking water laboratories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA developed multiple methods (example method numbers 314.0, 314.1, 314.2, 331.0, 332.0). Provide method descriptions and consider analytical costs; reference detailed method descriptions in the Occurrence and Monitoring Report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow Standardized Monitoring Framework (SMF) for Initial and Compliance Monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitoring frequency for public water systems depends on previous results, source water type, and waivers under the SMF (9-year compliance cycles divided into three 3-year periods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed initial monitoring: all ground water systems serving >10,000 persons and all surface water systems: quarterly within 12 months prior to compliance date (4 samples); ground water systems ≤10,000 persons: two samples within 12 months, second 5–7 months after first. States may allow previously acquired monitoring data to satisfy initial requirements. SMF allows State reduction to annual/triennial monitoring when system is 'reliably and consistently' below the MCL, though making such determinations can impose administrative burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic Monitoring Frequency Reduction via Binning Threshold (4.0 µg/L)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed binning approach: based on initial monitoring samples, systems with all sample concentrations ≤4.0 µg/L at an entry point automatically start at nine-year monitoring frequency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 4.0 µg/L selected because it was the MRL for UCMR 1; allows national applicability to ensure systems can reduce monitoring frequency. If any initial sample >4.0 µg/L but ≤ MCL, require annual (surface) or triennial (ground) monitoring; if any > MCL, require quarterly monitoring. States may require more frequent sampling for known sources or high variability. Automatic reduction is based only on initial monitoring samples collected prior to rule compliance date (including data from Jan 1, 2021 to publication of final rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: State Monitoring Waiver Criteria and Process
rubrics_metrics.description: States may grant monitoring waivers if conditions in 40 CFR 141.23(c)(3)-(6) are met; waiver requires multiple rounds of compliance sampling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surface water waiver: after three rounds of annual monitoring with results < MCL; ground water waiver: after three rounds of triennial monitoring with results < MCL. Systems on quarterly monitoring must first reduce to annual/triennial monitoring following a determination that system is 'reliably and consistently' below the MCL and conduct at least three rounds before applying. If approved, waiver must be in writing; sampling frequency cannot be less frequent than once every compliance cycle (9 years). At a minimum, one sample must be collected during the waiver effective term and waiver term cannot exceed one compliance cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of System MCL Violations via Initial and Confirmation Sample Average
rubrics_metrics.description: MCL violations determined based on the average of a compliance sample and a confirmation sample consistent with 40 CFR 141.23(i)(3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If initial sample ≤ MCL, compliance is based on that one sample. If initial sample > MCL, system must collect confirmation sample; compliance determined by averaging initial and confirmation values. Sample results are rounded to one significant figure prior to evaluation against the MCL. This approach is used instead of a running annual average because of the short sensitive exposure window (first trimester). EPA proposes confirmation sample be collected within five calendar days of notification of the first sample result and seeks comment on shorter (e.g., 3 days) or longer (e.g., 2 weeks) timeframes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing Requirements for Completing Initial Monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems must complete initial monitoring in anticipation of the rule compliance date; initial monitoring results inform compliance monitoring frequency after compliance date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under SDWA, NPDWRs generally take effect three years after promulgation (or amendment). Ground water systems >10,000 persons and all surface water systems must collect four samples per entry point over four consecutive quarters before compliance date. Ground water systems ≤10,000 persons must collect two samples within 12 months, 5–7 months apart, per entry point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Previously Collected Data to Satisfy Initial Monitoring (Cut-off Date)
rubrics_metrics.description: States can allow systems to use perchlorate data collected after January 1, 2021, to satisfy initial monitoring requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To qualify, historical data must have same number of samples required for initial monitoring (two or four) or be data collected under a State monitoring requirement. EPA set a cut-off date approx. six years prior to start of initial monitoring to ensure recent data; seeks comment on alternative cut-off dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow Composite Sampling with Triggered Follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: States may allow compositing (up to five samples combined) to reduce total number of analyses; reported concentration reflects average of contributing entry points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If composite concentration ≥ (MCL / number_of_samples), system must follow up with individual samples at each contributing sampling point. Example: with proposed MCL 20 µg/L, a five-sample composite would trigger follow-up if composite concentration ≥ 4 µg/L. Compositing can reduce costs but follow-up requirements apply when triggers exceeded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer Confidence Report (CCR) Content Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Community Water Systems (CWSs) must include specific perchlorate information in CCRs per SDWA Right to Know provisions and CCR Rule requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CCR must include MCL, MCLG, range of detected levels, highest detected level used to determine compliance, likely sources of perchlorate. If MCL violation occurs, CCR must include information about the violation, potential adverse health effects of perchlorate, and actions taken by the system to address the violation. Note: CCR Rule revisions in 2024 updated readability, delivery, and supplemental information requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider Administrative Burden When Determining State 'Reliably and Consistently' Decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that making determinations that a system is 'reliably and consistently' below the MCL can impose significant administrative burden on States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA anticipates many systems will have initial sample concentrations below proposed MCLs and that implementation will mainly require monitoring; explored limiting monitoring to likely-affected systems but could not find a reliable basis. Proposed automatic binning approach reduces need for per-system State determinations to lower administrative burden.
